text.tspan: Jocelyn: … I knew there was radio astronomy at Cambridge, but Cambridge was very prestigious I didn't expect to get in there, … so I put in
an application to Cambridge just in case and very much to my surprise, I got a place and it was quite terrifying going there. There were very
few women in Cambridge at that stage, … and I reckon they've made a mistake giving me a place, that I'm not bright enough, … and we now
Astrophysicist from Northern Ireland who, as a postgraduate student, discovered the first radio pulsars in 1967.
The discovery eventually earned the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1974; however, she was not one of the prize's recipients.
Chart on which Jocelyn Bell first recognised evidence
of a pulsar, exhibited at Cambridge University Library.
Jocelyn: … I had four foot of this chart paper, that's over a metre, every hour and I'm running 24 hours a day for six months. So I've got miles
of the stuff but just occasionally in these miles there was about five millimetres of signal that I couldn't understand. And the first few
times I logged it with a question mark and passed on because I've got metres of this flipping paper to get through. … but that was
the detection of the first pulsar.
Jocelyn: … so when I won this big, big prize [Breakthrough Prize in Fundamental Physics], the kind of alternative to the Nobel Prize,
I decided to put the money to allow people a bit like me, women and from other minorities to enable them to study for these PhDs,
these research degrees … to try and increase the diversity in physics departments.
recognise those feelings, we call it imposter syndrome. So I decided that I would work my very hardest so that when they threw me out, I wouldn't
have a guilty conscience I know I'd done my best. … so that was my approach from about day two in Cambridge. Well, the imposter syndrome led
me to be very, very thorough. So this is by now the third year of my PhD studies…
